title: Half a billion people, a few dozen engineers
teaches: A chat service: long-lived connections, delivery and read receipts, ordering in a conversation, message storage, presence and push

blocks.text: On 19 February 2014 Facebook agreed to buy WhatsApp for about $19 billion. The app was five years old. About 450 million people used it every month, and a month later Rick Reed, one of its engineers, told the Erlang Factory conference in San Francisco that the service was run by about 32 engineers. Two years earlier the team had posted a note on its blog with a screenshot of one server holding more than two million open connections at once, each one a phone waiting to be told about a new message.

A few engineers can carry that much traffic only if the design wastes nothing. Every request must do useful work, the system must avoid unnecessary copies, and each machine must operate near its capacity. In this lesson, we will design a chat service and compare it with what WhatsApp described and with what Discord, a chat service built for large communities, published about storing its messages in 2017 and again in 2023. Our target system serves **500 million people** who each send about **50 messages a day**, to one person or to groups. A message reaches an online phone in **under a second**, an offline phone receives the message when it reconnects, and the sender sees ticks for *sent*, *delivered* and *read*.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** Users can send a text message to one person or to a group of up to a few hundred members. The system shows the sender when the service has the message, when the recipient's phone has it, and when the recipient has opened it. It delivers messages to a phone that was offline when the message was sent, and keeps the messages in a conversation in a single order that every member sees. It also shows whether a contact is online and wakes a sleeping phone with a notification.

**Non-functional.** Delivery latency must be under a second from sender to an online recipient at the 99th percentile. Once the sender sees the first tick, the message is never lost. Messages are encrypted end to end, so the servers relay and store bytes they cannot read.[^e2e] That requirement rules out an entire class of features, because the server cannot search messages, filter them by content or generate link previews.

**Out of scope.** We will exclude voice and video calls, which are a separate problem involving jitter buffers and media relays. We also exclude photos and videos, which go to a blob store and a content delivery network (lesson 19) while the message carries only a link and a decryption key, as well as message history search and spam detection. We must also make one architectural choice early: whether the server keeps messages forever so a new phone can load years of history, or keeps them only until every recipient has received them. WhatsApp chose the second option, whereas Discord, whose channels are read by people who join later, had to choose the first.
Before drawing any system diagrams, we can calculate the traffic volume. Estimate the average message rate first, then move the sliders to see how the capacity numbers change.

blocks.caption: The estimate for a chat service, assuming about a third of users online at the evening peak and about 100 bytes of encrypted text per message.
blocks.task: Guess the rate, then try other sizes

blocks.text: Twenty-five billion messages a day is about 290,000 messages a second on average and perhaps 600,000 messages a second at the evening peak. That is a high write throughput, but a message is small, and 100 bytes times 25 billion is 2.5 TB of text a day, or under 1 PB a year. Storage is not the primary bottleneck. The harder problem is the number of phones online at once, which is about a third of 500 million users at the evening peak, or roughly 150 million concurrent devices. Each phone holds an open TCP connection, mostly idle, so the server can push a message the moment it arrives. The number of connections one server can hold determines the fleet size: at 2 million connections a server we need 75 machines, whereas at 50,000 connections a server we need 3,000 machines.

parts.title: Connections, the API and the data

blocks.text: In a naive design, each phone polls the server every few seconds to check for new messages. With 150 million phones polling every 5 seconds, the fleet handles 30 million requests a second, almost all answered "no", and a message still waits 2.5 seconds on average for the next poll. Polling consumes server capacity on empty checks. A **held connection** reverses this model. The phone opens one connection, using a WebSocket or a plain TCP socket with the app's own framing,[^websocket] and keeps it open so the server can write to it when a message arrives. An idle connection costs some kernel memory and a heartbeat packet every minute or so. You can use the workbench below to compare the two approaches.

The machines that hold connections are **gateways**. They terminate the transport encryption, authenticate the phone, and route messages to the internal network. Because a recipient's connection can be on any gateway, the service keeps a **session registry** in memory that maps each user to a gateway. A gateway writes to this table when a phone connects and refreshes the entry on each heartbeat, with a time-to-live (TTL) expiry so the entry for an abruptly disconnected phone expires automatically.

The API consists of a few frame types sent over that connection. **send**(conversation, client message id, ciphertext) returns **sent**(sequence number). The server pushes **message**(conversation, sequence number, sender, ciphertext). The phone answers **receipt**(conversation, sequence number, delivered or read). After a reconnect the phone sends **sync**(conversation, last sequence number seen) and receives everything after that number. The client message id is the idempotency key from lesson 22, ensuring that a phone sending the same message twice receives the same answer twice.

We design the data schema around the read patterns. Nearly every read requests either the latest few dozen messages in a conversation or all messages in a conversation after sequence number 41, so we store messages partitioned by **conversation** and sorted by sequence number. A database such as Cassandra splits its rows into **partitions** by a **partition key**, keeping each partition's rows together on the same few machines in sorted order, like the sorted map in lesson 10. A conversation that runs for years would create an oversized partition, so we add a **time bucket** to the partition key, such as (conversation, week) or (conversation, ten days), to bound the number of rows per partition. We do not store read receipts as one row per message per member; instead, each member has one pointer per conversation (such as "read up to 57") that the server overwrites as they read. Engineers choose the bucket duration so that the busiest conversation's bucket stays manageable, holding at most tens of thousands of messages. Quiet conversations then span many nearly empty buckets, which costs a few extra read operations when a user scrolls back. Discord chose a bucket duration of about ten days. When the system retains message history, deleting a message writes a **tombstone** marker over it, and the database removes the bytes later during compaction. With end-to-end encryption, "delete for everyone" also sends a small control message instructing each phone to remove its local copy.

Suppose Alice and Bob both send a message to a group at the same moment. Every phone in the group must display the two messages in the same order, and a phone reconnecting after losing signal in a tunnel must be able to request the exact messages it missed. We have four options for numbering messages: the sending phone's clock, the receiving gateway's clock, a single global counter for the whole service, or a per-conversation counter maintained by the server assigned to that conversation. Consider which option works best before revealing the clues that rule out the other three.

blocks.caption: How should messages in a conversation be ordered?
blocks.task: Guess, then show the clues one by one

ideas.name: The phone's clock
ideas.text: Each message carries the time on the phone that sent it.

ideas.name: The gateway's clock
ideas.text: The gateway that receives a message stamps it with its own time.

ideas.name: One global counter
ideas.text: A single counter numbers every message everywhere.

ideas.name: A per-conversation counter
ideas.text: Whichever server owns a conversation numbers its messages 1, 2, 3.

clues.name: Phones lie
clues.text: Phone clocks are often minutes wrong, and some users set them wrong on purpose.

clues.name: Two gateways, one moment
clues.text: Messages in one group arrive at different gateways, whose clocks differ by milliseconds (lesson 20), so two near-simultaneous messages can be stamped in either order.

clues.name: 600,000 a second
clues.text: One counter for every message on the service would be a single place taking 600,000 increments a second, and a single point of failure.

clues.name: Gaps show what's missing
clues.text: A phone that holds 41 and receives 43 knows 42 is missing, and can ask for it.

options.end: Only the conversation's own counter gives one order everyone agrees on, cheaply, with gaps a phone can see.

blocks.text: In this architecture, we assign each conversation an owner, which is a single process on one chat server at a time, chosen by hashing the conversation ID (lesson 5). The owner assigns sequence numbers to the conversation's messages. All traffic for a conversation passes through this single process, which easily handles the load because even a busy group sends only a few messages a second, and 600,000 messages a second spread across hundreds of millions of conversations is a light per-conversation rate. When we add a chat server, consistent hashing moves only a fraction of the conversations to it, and each moved conversation's new owner initializes its state the same way it would after a crash. If the owner's machine fails, another server takes over the conversation, reads the latest sequence number from the database, and resumes numbering. To make that handover safe against split-brain writes, the database write must be conditional on the sequence number not already existing, using the fencing mechanism from lesson 11.

We can now trace a single message from Alice's phone to the conversation owner, which assigns a sequence number and writes the message to the database before returning a "sent" receipt, and then pushes the message through Bob's gateway to his phone and returns the delivery and read receipts. We also need to handle two failure cases: when Bob's phone is offline, and when Alice's acknowledgement is lost in transit.

blocks.caption: One message from Alice to Bob, time running down the page: blue requests, green answers, orange a write to the store. Times are round milliseconds for a phone on a good connection.
blocks.task: Play the case where Bob's phone is off

blocks.text: The first tick indicates that the message is durably stored, not merely received by a gateway, because a gateway crashing between sending the receipt and writing to the database would lose a message the sender believed was safe. When Bob's phone is offline, no data is lost and the sender does not need to retry: the message waits in the database, the chat service asks Apple's or Google's push service to wake the phone,[^apns] and the phone reconnects and requests all messages after sequence number 41. When Alice's acknowledgement is lost, her phone resends the message with the same client message ID, and the owner recognises the duplicate ID and returns the existing sequence number instead of writing a second copy.

You can now adjust the primary architectural parameters in the workbench to see how throughput, latency and server costs respond. The model assumes evening peak traffic: 150 million phones online, 600,000 messages a second sent, and 30% of those messages sent to groups. We estimate server costs at $400 a month per machine.

blocks.caption: The delivery path at the evening peak. A wire's width and its label give the rate on it; the gateway count follows the connections each server holds.
blocks.task: Find settings that deliver in under a second with the fewest store writes

blocks.text: The model highlights three trade-offs. Polling every 30 seconds requires fewer servers than polling every 5 seconds, but increases average delivery latency to 15 seconds; only a held connection achieves both low server load and sub-second delivery. The number of connections per server determines the gateway fleet size, requiring 1,500 gateways at 100,000 connections per server, or 75 gateways at WhatsApp's density of 2 million connections per server. Finally, writing a separate copy of a message for each group member multiplies database write throughput by the group size, whereas storing one copy per conversation plus one read pointer per member writes each message once. Live delivery to online group members still requires network fan-out, pushing one copy down each recipient's open connection, but storing a single copy per conversation eliminates the storage write fan-out (lesson 14).

**When a gateway fails**, every phone connected to it detects the dropped connection and reconnects to another gateway. At 2 million connections per server, a single machine failure triggers 2 million TLS handshakes (the cryptographic key exchange that sets up encryption at the start of every secure connection). Each handshake consumes about 1 ms of CPU time across the surviving fleet, and phones whose connection attempts time out will retry and increase the load further. To prevent a cascading failure, clients must wait a random backoff interval of tens of seconds before reconnecting (the jitter technique from lesson 18), and the gateways must rate-limit incoming connection handshakes (lesson D1). Synchronising by sequence number keeps the post-connection data transfer small, because each phone requests only messages newer than its last recorded sequence number rather than reloading the entire conversation. Higher connection density per server increases the magnitude of this reconnection spike, which is the operational trade-off of holding 2 million connections on one machine.

**Presence** uses the session registry in reverse. A phone's periodic heartbeat keeps its session registry entry alive, and when the entry expires, the system marks the user offline. Pushing a status update to every contact the moment a user connects creates a large notification fan-out on every connection event, so most services push presence updates only to contacts who currently have a chat with that user open on screen, while other contacts query the user's status only when they open the conversation. Live location sharing uses the same pattern: the service overwrites the user's latest coordinates in memory every few seconds with a short TTL, pushes updates over the open connections of users currently viewing the map, and appends the coordinates to a persistent log (lesson 16) only if the feature requires location history.

**Notifications** become a separate subsystem once an application supports multiple delivery channels. Upstream services write notification events ("tell user X about Y") to a message log, and channel-specific worker processes consume from the log to call external providers such as Apple's and Google's push services, SMS gateways, or email servers. Before calling a provider, the workers check the user's notification preferences and quiet hours, deduplicate events using an idempotency key, and enforce a per-user rate limit so a software bug cannot flood a user with thousands of alerts. Isolating each channel in its own worker pool ensures that an outage at one external provider backs up only that channel's queue, allowing urgent notifications to fail over to an alternative channel.

WhatsApp's engineers wrote their servers in **Erlang**, a language developed at Ericsson in the 1980s for telephone switches in which each connection runs as its own lightweight process,[^erlang] and ran them on FreeBSD, tuning the operating system kernel until a single machine could hold over 2 million open connections. Their architecture minimised the server's responsibilities. The servers stored messages only until the recipient's phone acknowledged delivery, and then deleted them, keeping long-term message history solely on the client devices. Because the servers never had to answer queries for historical messages from years earlier, WhatsApp needed no long-term message database, and enabling end-to-end encryption across all chats in 2016 did not break any server-side features.

Discord made the opposite retention choice because users joining a large community channel expect to read years of prior messages. In a 2017 engineering post, Discord described migrating billions of messages from MongoDB to Cassandra using the composite partition key (channel id, bucket), where a bucket spans a fixed 10-day window of timestamp-based message IDs and rows are sorted by message ID within each partition. However, extreme traffic outliers eventually strained this setup: the busiest channel on a large community server routed so many concurrent reads to the same few Cassandra nodes that those nodes fell behind, while frequent message deletions left tombstone markers that slowed down range scans.[^tombstone] In 2023, Discord described migrating from 177 Cassandra nodes to a 72-node ScyllaDB cluster and placing a Rust data-service layer in front of the database to coalesce identical concurrent reads for a hot channel into a single database query, using the request coalescing pattern from lesson 15.

Comparing the two architectures with our design exercise shows that both services converged on held connections, per-conversation ordering, and a composite (conversation, time bucket) partition key. The decision that caused the largest divergence in infrastructure was a product requirement rather than a low-level technical mechanism: whether to retain message history on the server. By deleting messages upon delivery, WhatsApp eliminated an entire storage tier from its architecture.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **Handling ten times the message throughput** becomes necessary mainly when supporting much larger groups rather than more users. A community channel with 1 million members cannot push every incoming message over 1 million open connections in real time. Instead, the service pushes live messages only to members who currently have that channel open on screen, while inactive members fetch the latest messages from the database when they open the channel, applying the hybrid fan-out-on-read approach that lesson 14 used for social media accounts with millions of followers. **Supporting multiple devices per user** also multiplies traffic, turning one recipient into four. Each device maintains its own read pointer, and under end-to-end encryption each device holds its own cryptographic keys, requiring the sender's phone to encrypt the message payload separately for each of the recipient's registered devices.

**Scaling to a hundred times the traffic across global regions** places members of the same conversation on different continents. Each user connects to a regional gateway near them, while each conversation's owner process runs in one specific region, so a message sent between Sydney and London crosses an intercontinental undersea link once, adding about 150 ms of network latency. Dynamically migrating a conversation's owner process to the region holding the majority of its active members, and replicating stored messages across regions so a datacentre outage never loses an acknowledged message, are the next engineering challenges at global scale.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on a chat service
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: 150 million phones are online at once. Why do chat services hold a connection open instead of having phones poll every 5 seconds?
choices: Polling every 5 seconds would mean about 30 million requests a second, nearly all of them answered no, and messages waiting 2.5 s
Phones can't open a new connection every 5 seconds, because their radios need about a minute to wake up and settle again
A held connection is encrypted end to end, while a polling request can only ever be encrypted in transit
items.why: 150 million ÷ 5 s is 30 million requests a second, and a message still waits half a poll interval on average. A held connection lets the server push messages immediately.

items.ask: Why number messages with a counter per conversation instead of each phone's clock?
choices: Phone clocks can't be read by the server once the message has been encrypted end to end on the phone
A counter is shorter than a timestamp
One owner's counter gives a single order, and a missing number shows as a gap
items.why: Phone clocks are often minutes wrong. Numbering messages 1, 2, 3 at the conversation's owner gives an order everyone agrees on, and a phone holding messages 41 and 43 knows to request message 42.

items.ask: Alice's phone sends a message, the service stores it, and the "sent" acknowledgement is lost. Alice's phone sends again. What keeps Bob from seeing it twice?
choices: The gateway drops any message that arrives twice within one second from the same phone
The message carries a client id; the owner recognises it and returns the same sequence number
Bob's phone compares the text of each new message with the last one and hides repeats
items.why: The client message id is an idempotency key. The owner stores the message once and answers a duplicate request with the sequence number it already assigned, making the resend harmless.

items.ask: Bob's phone was off for an hour and reconnects. What does an efficient design send it?
choices: Every message in every one of his conversations, so the phone can rebuild its view
Nothing until he opens a conversation, which then loads its whole history from the start
For each conversation, the messages numbered after the last sequence number the phone has
items.why: Using sequence-number synchronisation, the phone reports the last sequence number it received, and the server sends only newer messages. Reconnecting requires work proportional only to the messages missed.

items.ask: Messages are stored with the partition key (conversation, ten-day bucket), sorted by message id. Why the bucket?
choices: It bounds each partition's size, however long the conversation runs
It lets the store delete a whole bucket once every member of the conversation has read the messages inside it
It spreads one conversation's newest messages across many nodes, so that writes never have to queue
items.why: Reads query a conversation's latest messages, so the conversation ID comes first in the partition key; the time bucket prevents a long-running conversation from growing into a partition that is too large to manage.

items.ask: A gateway holding 2 million connections dies. What should the design do so the rest of the fleet survives?
choices: Have every phone reconnect at once, so that the outage is as short as it can possibly be
Keep a standby gateway with a copy of every connection
Random waits before reconnecting, and a rate limit on new connections
items.why: Two million TLS handshakes in one second would overload the surviving gateways and trigger retry storms. Randomised backoff (jitter) spreads the reconnection attempts over time, and a rate limit on new connections protects the gateways.

items.ask: A group has 1,000 members. Which design stores each message most cheaply while still showing everyone the right unread count?
choices: One copy per conversation, and for each member one pointer to the last message they have read
One copy in every member's own inbox, so that each member can read their messages fastest
One copy per member who is online, and none for members who are offline at the time
items.why: Copying the message into every member's inbox writes 1,000 rows per message. Storing one copy per conversation plus a "read up to n" pointer per member writes the message once while still tracking each member's unread count.

summary: **Hold connections instead of polling.** 150 million phones polling every 5 seconds generates 30 million mostly empty requests a second, whereas an idle held connection costs only kernel memory and a periodic heartbeat.

**Gateways hold connections and a registry locates them.** The session registry maps each connected user to their current gateway, refreshed by heartbeats and expiring automatically when heartbeats stop.

**A per-conversation counter establishes a single order.** The conversation's assigned owner process numbers its messages sequentially, ensuring that every member sees the same order and any gap reveals a missing message.
**Write to durable storage before acknowledging "sent".** The first tick guarantees that the message is stored on disk, and a client message ID makes retries idempotent.

**Offline phones synchronise by sequence number.** The message waits in the database, a push notification wakes the phone, and the client requests all messages after its last recorded sequence number.
**Partition the database by conversation and time bucket.** Queries fetch the latest messages in a single conversation, and the time bucket bounds the size of each database partition.
**Store read receipts as pointers.** Maintain one "read up to n" pointer per member per conversation rather than writing a receipt row for every message and reader.

**Protect against reconnection storms.** When a failed gateway drops millions of connections at once, clients must apply randomised backoff (jitter) and surviving gateways must rate-limit new connection handshakes.

**Message retention policy drives the storage architecture.** WhatsApp deleted messages after delivery and needed no long-term message store, whereas Discord retained all history and had to scale Cassandra and later ScyllaDB.

e2e.title: End-to-end encryption
e2e.text: With end-to-end encryption only the phones hold the keys; the servers see ciphertext plus who sent what to whom and when. WhatsApp turned it on for every chat in April 2016, using the Signal protocol from Open Whisper Systems. Metadata still reaches the server, and is still worth protecting.

websocket.title: WebSocket
websocket.text: A **WebSocket** (RFC 6455, 2011) starts as an HTTP request that asks to upgrade, then becomes a two-way stream of framed messages on the same TCP connection. Browsers support it, which is why web chat uses it; mobile apps often use their own framing over TCP or QUIC instead.

apns.title: Push services
apns.text: A phone's operating system keeps one connection open to Apple's Push Notification service or Google's Firebase Cloud Messaging for every app on it, so each app doesn't need its own. A server sends a small payload, a few kilobytes at most, to that service, which wakes the phone; the app then connects and fetches the real message.

erlang.title: A process per phone
erlang.text: Erlang processes are not operating-system threads. They are managed by the Erlang runtime, start with a few hundred words of memory, and share nothing, passing messages to each other. Millions can run on one machine, so "one process per connection" is a natural design rather than an extravagance, and a crash in one process takes down only that connection.

tombstone.title: Tombstones
tombstone.text: In a log-structured store (lesson 10) a delete can't erase data already written to an immutable file, so it writes a marker, a **tombstone**, that hides the old value until compaction removes both. A read over a range with many deletes has to step over every tombstone in it, which is how a channel where many messages were deleted can make reads slow.
